Just now

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

The AI wasn’t slow. I was. I had to sit and watch it, and that watching was the whole job.
It was a Thursday afternoon and I had six things open. A Claude Code session churning through a database migration in one window. A half-written spec in another. An AI engineer pinging me about a preview that looked wrong. Two browser tabs of docs I meant to read an hour ago. And in the corner of my eye, always, the terminal, because if I looked away for four minutes the session would confidently do something I did not ask for and I would have to unwind it.
So I did not look away. I sat there, hand near the keyboard, approving steps, reading diffs half as fast as they scrolled, ready to hit stop the second it went sideways. That is what the afternoon was. Not building. Watching a thing build, and being the only reason it did not wander off.
I remember the exact moment it clicked. The migration finished, and I realized I had spent forty minutes producing nothing except my own attention. The AI had done the work. I had done the babysitting. And the babysitting was the bottleneck.
The AI was fast. The handoff was not.
Here is the thing nobody warns you about when you go all-in on AI coding. The model is quick. Genuinely quick. It can scaffold a feature faster than I can describe it. The slow part is me: the approving, the reviewing, the catching, the re-explaining when it drifts.
Every run needed a human in the loop, and the human was a single person with one set of eyes. I could kick off a task, but I could not leave. If I left, it would keep going anyway, which was worse. As one builder on Reddit put it, exactly the way I felt it: “it steamrolls ahead anyway.” Helpful, in the way a firehose is helpful.
We were using AI to build our own tools, and we kept hitting the same wall. We could think in parallel. We could not build in parallel, because building meant one of us tethered to one session, watching.
So the real cost was not compute. It was human time. Every hour of “progress” had an hour of me stapled to it. If a teammate needed that much supervision to not go rogue, you would not call them autonomous. You would call them an intern who cannot be left alone.
We could think in six directions and build in one.
The queue was the quiet killer. We would line up work: build this, then that, then the other thing. Not because the tasks depended on each other, but because each one needed a babysitter, and we only had so many babysitters.
So I would hand a session one thing to build, then wait. The next thing could not start until this one finished, not for any technical reason, but because I was the shared resource and I was busy watching. We could hold six ideas in our heads at once. We could only pour attention into one lane at a time.
The waiting between builds was where the day quietly went. Not in dramatic blocks. In fifteen-minute slivers of “I will just keep half an eye on this before I start the next one.” Those slivers added up to the whole afternoon, and at the end of it we had shipped one thing instead of six.
That is the specific pain that made us stop and build something. Not “the AI is bad.” The AI was fine. The workflow around it made me the constraint, and I was the most expensive part.
So we built the lanes we wished we had.
DevKanban started as an answer to exactly that afternoon. It is an AI-native development workflow, and its core primitive is the card. A card is a fully isolated workstream: its own git branch, created automatically, its own dedicated cloud environment, its own instant preview URL. Parallel cards do not share state. You can run several at once and they do not touch each other.
The point of the isolation is not tidiness. It is that a card can run unattended. I kick it off, I walk away, I go work on something else, and it does not need me hovering to keep it honest. When I come back, there is a preview URL with something real behind it, not a terminal frozen on a permission prompt waiting for a human who wandered off.
That is the flip. Before, every run was tethered to my attention. Now the lane runs on its own, and my attention is a thing I spend on the parts that actually need judgment, at the start when I write the brief and at the end when I look at what came back.
But isolation alone was not enough. A lane you can leave alone is dangerous if nothing is watching for quality while you are gone. So the second half of the answer is Firebat.
Firebat is the thing that watches so I do not have to.
Firebat is the harness inside every card. Harness engineering is a standard practice, not something we invented: it means building structure around a model’s calls so the output comes back reliable instead of random. Firebat is our specific version of it. It defines what good output looks like for a given task, validates the work against that definition, and catches failures before they propagate downstream.
That last part is what let me stop babysitting. The reason I sat there watching was fear: fear it would break something and I would not notice until it had broken ten more things on top of it. The “fix-one-break-ten” dread is real, and it is why so many people cannot leave the room. Firebat is what I hold the tooling to instead of holding my own eyeballs to the screen.
We felt the difference the first month, because we were dogfooding hard. Our rule was blunt: we build everything in the thing before we release it. We spent the past month running our own development, including DevKanban’s own, inside DevKanban. That is how we found the bug that would have sunk us.
The merge that bled, and why we caught it.
We had several cards active at once, which was the whole point. One of them held a fix that got merged. And that just-merged fix bled into a still-running card’s preview, because the environment was not fully sealed after the merge.
Read that again, because it is the exact failure a parallel user would hit constantly. You are running three lanes, you merge one, and it silently contaminates the other two. The previews you are comparing are no longer honest. You would be “comparing vibes instead of evidence” without even knowing the evidence was corrupted.
We caught it because we were depending on the tool for real work, not demoing it for a screenshot. When your own afternoon breaks, you fix it before you ever let a customer near it. We sealed the environment properly after merge, and now the isolation actually holds under the exact condition that matters.
That bug is the best argument I have for dogfooding. A tool that ran fine in a clean demo would ship this fragility straight to users. We only found it because we lived inside it.
The test we hold the AI to now.
Somewhere in that month, our internal standard for the tooling settled into one sentence, and it turned out founders on Reddit had independently landed on the same test: does it save time, ship something, or replace human time in the next thirty days? If not, cut it. Earn its seat like a teammate.
The babysitting version of AI failed that test for me. It helped me start faster and then quietly charged me back the time in supervision. “Does it finish the job, or just help me start faster” is the question that matters, and half-watching a run all afternoon is not finishing the job. It is renting my attention to a machine that is faster than me at everything except knowing when it is wrong.
The unattended-lane version passes. I kick off a card, I leave, Firebat holds the line while I am gone, and I come back to real progress instead of a paused prompt. The human time that used to be stapled to every run is mine again. That is not a speed feature. It is the difference between the AI being a tool I operate and a tool that operates while I do something else.
We are not trying to make the model faster. It is already faster than us. We are building the structure that lets us stop being the bottleneck standing next to it.
So here is my actual question, because I want a real answer, not a vibe. When you use AI to build, are you the bottleneck? Sit with your last long session and count honestly: how much of that time was the AI working, and how much was you watching it so it would not wander off? If you subtract the watching, what is your day actually made of?
